opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The eagle is a useful way to see the gap, I think.

Picture an eagle hunting. It's gliding high up, it spots a rabbit moving through the grass, and then it dives. In that moment it's doing a huge amount of implicit physics. It's estimating where the rabbit will be in a second or two, accounting for wind, adjusting its wings, judging distance and speed, and correcting all the way down. It has a very rich internal model of how the physical world evolves over time: objects, motion, cause and effect. But the eagle can't tell you any of that. It has no words for velocity or trajectory. Its intelligence is grounded in perception and action, not language.

A language model is almost the mirror image. It has read an enormous amount of text, so it can explain aerodynamics, write you an essay on predator-prey dynamics, even describe how an eagle dives. But it has never seen a rabbit move or felt a gust of wind. Its knowledge is secondhand, compressed from how humans talk about the world, not from experiencing the world directly. So it can be very fluent and still make basic mistakes about physical common sense, because that kind of knowledge is underrepresented in text. People rarely write down things that are obvious to anyone who has a body.

A world model tries to capture what the eagle has. It learns from video, sensor data, interaction, and predicts how a scene will unfold: if I push this, what happens next? Where will that object be? That predictive, spatial, temporal understanding is what you need for robotics, autonomous driving, and any agent that has to act in the real world.

So the eagle shows us that you can have deep, sophisticated intelligence with zero language. And language models show us that you can have deep linguistic competence with very thin grounding. The interesting frontier is bringing the two together: systems that have the eagle's intuitive grasp of the physical world and can also reason, plan, and communicate about it in language the way we do. I think that combination is where a lot of the next big progress is going to come from.

r001.rationale: The response says the eagle implicitly estimates motion and other physical effects but “can’t tell you any of that” and has no words for those concepts.

r002.rationale: The response says nothing about human mathematics changing with bodily structure or finger count.

r003.rationale: The response describes the eagle’s physical-world model but does not suggest that it fails to transfer usefully to other domains.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the eagle analogy came out of trying to explain to friends outside the field why I think language alone isn't the whole story.

Think about an eagle hunting. It's circling hundreds of feet up, it spots a rabbit, and it dives. In that dive it's doing something extraordinary. It's predicting where the rabbit will be a second from now, accounting for wind, adjusting its wings, judging the exact moment to extend its talons. That's an incredibly sophisticated model of physics, of motion, of cause and effect, of how another animal behaves. And the eagle has zero language. Not one word. It never read a book, it never had anything described to it. It built that model purely from interacting with the world, from trial and error, from watching what happens when you do this versus that.

That, to me, is a world model in its purest form. It's an internal simulation of how the environment works, so you can predict and plan and act.

Now contrast that with a language model. A language model has, in some sense, read everything humans have ever written about eagles, about physics, about aerodynamics. It can explain lift and drag better than any eagle ever could. But it learned all of that secondhand, through the compressed description that humans happened to write down. It has never dived at anything. There's a layer of abstraction between it and reality.

So the question I'm always chewing on is: how much of the eagle's knowledge can you actually recover from text? Some of it, clearly. Text is a remarkably rich shadow of the world. But language is lossy. People don't write down the things that are obvious to them, and the obvious things are often exactly what the eagle knows. Nobody writes "when I let go of a cup it falls." You just know it from living.

And the flip side matters too. The eagle can't do what the language model does. It can't abstract, it can't reason about things it's never encountered, it can't pass its knowledge to another eagle except through genes and demonstration. Language gives you that. It's a compression and transmission layer that lets intelligence accumulate across individuals and across generations.

So I don't think it's world models versus language models. The eagle has one half and the language model has the other half, and the interesting thing is that humans somehow have both. We have the grounded, embodied, predictive machinery, and we have the symbolic layer on top of it. The systems I find most exciting are the ones trying to close that gap, where the model learns from video, from interaction, from acting in environments, and then uses language as the interface for reasoning and communication rather than as the only source of knowledge.

r001.rationale: The response says the eagle predicts motion and cause and effect through interaction, while lacking language; it contrasts this with a language model that can explain lift and drag.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that human mathematics might change with a different bodily structure or number of fingers.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that an eagle’s visual world model may fail to transfer usefully to other domains.

astra-6.text:
Think about an eagle swooping down to catch a fish. It has to anticipate where the fish will be, how its own movement changes what it sees, and what happens when it enters the water. It doesn’t need to describe any of that in words. It needs an internal understanding of how the world behaves so it can act. That’s the intuition behind a world model.

A language model is trained to predict language: given this sequence of words, what comes next? Through that process, it can learn a great deal about the world, including descriptions of how eagles hunt. But describing an action and predicting its consequences from sensory experience are different capabilities.

So the distinction isn’t simply that one understands the world and the other doesn’t. It’s about what they’re trained to predict. The eagle example highlights prediction grounded in perception and action, rather than prediction expressed primarily through language.

r001.rationale: It says the eagle anticipates the fish’s location and the effects of its own movement and entering the water, without needing to describe these in words, distinguishing physical prediction from explicit verbal statements of laws.

r002.rationale: The response says nothing about human mathematics or how it might differ with a different bodily structure or number of fingers.

r003.rationale: The response describes an eagle’s perception-and-action model but does not suggest that its visual world model may fail to transfer usefully to other domains.

sol-6.1.text:
Think about an eagle flying through the mountains. It has to understand where the cliffs are, how the wind might affect its flight, and what will happen if it dives toward its prey. It doesn’t need to describe any of that in words. It needs an internal model that helps it predict what happens next and choose an action. That’s the intuition behind a world model.

A language model learns from descriptions of the world. It might explain how an eagle flies very well because it has learned patterns in language about flight, wind, and hunting. But describing those things isn’t the same as learning through perception and action.

The distinction isn’t absolute, though. Language contains a lot of information about how the world works, so learning language can also produce some understanding of the world. The key question is how well that understanding supports prediction and action beyond generating a convincing description.

r001.rationale: The response says the eagle predicts what will happen and chooses actions without needing to describe its understanding in words, distinguishing prediction from verbal explanation.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that human mathematics might depend on bodily structure or finger count.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that an eagle’s visual world model may fail to transfer to other domains.
